c: Music in Ancient Israel
The earliest nomadic peoples made music. The first musician mentioned in the Bible is “Jubal, the first of all who play the harp and flute” (
). Music was significant from the beginning of Israel’s worship in the Tabernacle. In
, Aaron’s robe is described as having bells attached to the lower hem that sounded as he entered the Holy Place. Scripture records several songs created by the people of God (e.g.,
The first liturgical music mentioned in the Old Testament is in the narrative of the transfer of the Ark—David and the Israelites sang, played instruments, and danced to the glory of the Lord (
). David is recognized as making the musical instruments used in the Temple (
). In the postexilic era, the Levitical singers that are mentioned were the descendants of Asaph, the chief musician appointed by David (
). In short, Israel’s liturgical music and organization originated in the time of David.
The stately ceremony of the later services in Solomon’s Temple contrasts with the enthusiasm and spontaneity of David’s worship (
). Singers and musicians for worship at the Temple were chosen from the tribe of Levi (
). They rotated their participation in the weekday, Sabbath, and high holy day services.

This untitled lament by an aging believer is more of a confession of confidence and hope than the cry of someone abandoned by God. The psalmist experienced God’s power and protection in his youth (
) and now prays for rescue from the adversaries who stalk him in his old age (
). Even in the midst of his peril, he continues to tell of God’s past faithfulness and looks forward with hope to a time when he can testify to the next generation that God is faithful and righteous.
